docTitle.titlePart: Towards AI-assisted discovery in papyrology: Searching unpublished texts with Anagnostes

div.note: The authors thank Graham Claytor and Holger Essler for their useful comments and suggestions.

div.head: 1 Introduction
div.p: With the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), various research initiatives have emerged that apply this new digital technology specifically to the study of Greek papyri. To name just a few, the project ‘EGRAPSA: Retracing the evolutions of handwritings in Greco-Roman Egypt thanks to digital palaeography’ applies computational methods to the analysis of palaeography of papyri. Within the framework of the project ‘The crocodile and human mummies of Tebtunis: AI-supported reconstruction and edition of the Hellenistic papyri of the Bancroft Library (Berkeley)’, machine learning (ML) will be used to match fragments belonging to the same document. The Vesuvius Challenge project has achieved the virtual unrolling of carbonised Herculaneum scrolls and the recovery of text from them using machine learning. A pipeline for producing digital-born editions of Coptic Manichaean codices, Herculaneum philosophical texts, and Latin wooden tablets is being developed as part of the project ‘AI Models with Reinforcement Learning to Edit text in Damaged Manuscripts’.
In this article, we present new possibilities for searching digitised collections of papyri and for papyrological discovery using the new AI-driven system Anagnostes.

Anagnostes is the first handwritten text recognition (HTR) tool which can automatically transcribe Greek papyri from images with sufficient accuracy for a range of papyrological tasks. It is specifically designed to handle cursive handwriting in Greek documentary papyri from Ptolemaic, Roman, and Late Antique Egypt, whose transcription has traditionally required highly specialised papyrological expertise and years of training. The tool has been specifically trained to transcribe damaged and fragmentary texts.

Anagnostes was developed by Elena Chepel and Anton Repushko in July-August 2026 and released as an online demo on 4 September 2026. A group of volunteers helped manually annotate approximately 600 papyri, and all annotations were checked by E. Chepel.

The training dataset comprises images of published papyri retrieved from publicly available NAKALA and Berlin Papyrus Database collections and aligned with the texts of editions encoded on papyri.info. We would like to thank the developers and contributors of these online resources without whose work the training would not have been possible.

The training dataset includes documentary and literary papyrus fragments from Ptolemaic, Roman, and Late Antique Egypt. The texts selected for annotation were chosen partly by E. Chepel and partly by the volunteers themselves.

The architecture of the tool was designed by A. Repushko, who did also model development. Anagnostes is an end-to-end system consisting of several transformer models, each performing a different task: a layout recognition pipeline for line segmentation; a HTR model trained to recognise letters and symbols; and a model trained on the corpus of texts on papyri.info to handle word division and supplement short lacunae of two to three letters.

All components of the system are modular and can be replaced with alternative models, if better solutions become available. Each component can also be updated through further training. A full description of the new version of the system, incorporating improvements based on lessons learned from the current demo version, will be published in 2027 in a co-authored article by A. Repushko and E. Chepel. The publication will include the training and evaluation datasets, the code, the model weights, and detailed metrics documenting the system’s performance.

In the present article, we demonstrate how Anagnostes, even in its current version, can contribute to papyrological research. We describe the process of AI-assisted searching for unpublished material in several collections accessible online and present a number of discoveries made possible by this search, including five new fragments from collections in Vienna, Yale, and Bonn. Before presenting the search methods implemented in our study (section 4), we discuss the quality of the transcriptions produced by Anagnostes (section 2) and the nature of the resulting corpus of texts used for the search (section 3).

div.head: 2 The accuracy of automated transcriptions generated by Anagnostes
div.p:
HTR, sometimes referred to also as Optical Character Recognition (OCR) or Automated Text Recognition (ATR), is a well-established area of Computer Sciences (CS) and forms part of the broader fields of computer vision and document analysis and recognition.
See, for example, Proceedings of the International Conference on Document Analysis and Recognition (ICDAR), which has been held since 1991. In recent years, various types of AI models have increasingly been trained for HTR tasks.
E.g. pretrained transformer models (TrOCR) adapted to medieval manuscripts, see Sharma et al. 2027; for a comparison between CRNN networks and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for Arabic scripts, see Vidal-Gorène et al., forthcoming.

Within computer science (CS) and the digital humanities, transcription accuracy is assessed using a set of standard metrics, of which Character Error Rate (CER) is one of the most widely used and informative. CER measures the percentage of characters that differ between an AI-generated transcription and a human-verified reference (the ‘ground-truth’). For example, a CER of 20.0% corresponds to five character errors per 25 characters in the reference text, assuming no insertions or deletions beyond those five errors.
For a more detailed explanation, see the guidelines for calculating CER provided by Transkribus, one of the leading platforms for the automated recognition of handwritten historical documents.

CERs achieved by modern HTR models vary depending on the document type, condition, and script. While CERs for modern printed text can be as low as 0.5-1%, Transkribus reports CERs of 5-15% for its models applied to medieval manuscripts. Similarly, CoMMA, an AI-transcribed corpus of more than 32,000 medieval Latin and Old French manuscripts, has an average CER of 9.7% (Clérice et al. 2026: §4.3). The CoMMA website warns users that the error varies between 6% and 25%, with even less reliable results for particularly challenging documents featuring cursive writing, damaged pages, or poor digitisation quality.

This context is important for understanding the accuracy of text recognition in Greek papyri, which pose even greater challenges than the relatively uniform handwriting found in medieval manuscripts. The current average CER of Anagnostes is 17.9%, with best pieces achieving CERs as low as 2-8%. We calculated the average CER using a ground-truth dataset comprising 55 papyri and a total of 912 lines.
For this evaluation dataset, papyri were selected automatically from our annotated dataset. The proportions of papyri of different sizes (measured by the number of lines) and from different historical periods are the same as in the training dataset. All papyri included in the evaluation dataset can be viewed in the graph on the Papybench website. Of these, 374 lines have a CER below 10%, while 34 of the 55 papyri in the validation dataset have CERs between 10 and 25%.

The fragments recognised most accurately are literary texts, documents in clear handwriting, with minimal surface damage, and high-resolution digitisation. The highest error dates occur in texts written in highly cursive, heavily-abbreviated, and late hands, such as 7th–8th cent. accounts, in severely damaged fragments, and in low-quality images. With additional training data, the CER of Anagnostes is expected to improve in the updated version.

CER is also directly affected by inaccuracies introduced at earlier stages of the pipeline, particularly, during layout recognition, since the HTR model can only recognise characters included in the segmented lines. An evaluation of Anagnostes’ line detection performance under the current pipeline design will be discussed in a forthcoming article by O. Donath and H. Essler.

Transkribus distinguishes between target CERs for different use cases. According to Transkribus, a CER below 2% is sufficiently low to allow an automatic transcription to be published in a critical edition with minimal review, while a CER of 5-8% is suitable for full-text search and a CER of 10-15% is acceptable for keyword spotting.

We have evaluated how different CERs in automated transcriptions affect the efficiency of searching and classifying Greek papyri, using the corpus of published texts available on papyri.info (see the preprint currently under review at IJDAR: Repushko and Chepel, forthcoming). The tolerance of noisy OCR in historical text analysis has previously been investigated for other types of documents, but not for Greek papyri. (Hamdi et al. 2023; Hill and Hengchen 2019). This tolerance varies depending on the language, its grammatical structure, word length, and text structure.

In the article submitted to IJDAR, our aim was to demonstrate, using mathematical methods and quantitative analysis, that search tasks can be successfully performed even with the current CER of Anagnostes. In the present article, we assess the tool’s performance and search efficiency qualitatively, illustrating them with several examples of previously unidentified papyrus texts discovered during our experimental searches.

div.head: 3 AI-transcribed corpora: a new type of text and a new research opportunity
div.p:
Scholarly work on written objects, such as papyri and inscriptions, has traditionally involved two forms of the existence of a text – the original and the edition. Until recently, the text of most unpublished documents and manuscripts could be consulted only through a digital image or by autopsy. The labour of (re)establishing the text of the original and presenting it, together with the editorial layer, in a format accessible by both humans (text printed according to the Leiden conventions) and machines (text encoded in XML and added to papyri.info) is a crucial part of the papyrologist’s profession.
On the human / printed text part, see Youtie 1963 and 1966.

New technologies now make it possible to make a third form of text between the original and the published edition – an automated first-pass transcription layer – accessible at scale. While a CER above 10% is nowhere near the standards of scholarly editions, these preliminary transcriptions still offer researchers far greater opportunities to work with unpublished papyri than digital images alone.

A recent example of a historical discovery made using an AI-transcribed corpus has been presented by Benjamen Breen, a historian of science and medicine and a professor of history at the University of California (Breen 2026). By searching a five-million-page archive of documents from the Dutch East India Company, he was able to identify a previously unnoticed Dutch account of dodo hunting dating to 1615. These historical documents have been made searchable and accessible using state-of-the-art HTR software trained specifically on this material. Within the following few days, further discoveries were made in the same corpus by extending Breen’s approach and using AI assistants to guide the search.

This progress, while beneficial to research, must nevertheless be approached with caution, as there is a risk that some users may uncritically regard corpora of automatically transcribed texts as being as reliable as scholarly editions. Thibault Clérice, one of the authors of CoMMA, discussed this risk in his keynote lecture, “The Transcription/Edition Distinction as a Foundation for Trustworthy Automatic Text Recognition,” delivered at the SCOOP meeting in Vienna in September 2026: “When text establishment is silently delegated to an undocumented, unverified machine process, the resulting corpus ceases to be a reliable scientific source yet is treated as one.”

At the same time, Clérice argues that the conflation of transcription and edition is not in itself new; rather, ATR systems merely industrialise an ambiguity that already exists in the preliminary transcription of unpublished texts. The difference introduced by modern technologies is that the edition is no longer the sole publicly available text, as it once was. An imperfect pre-editorial transcription ceases to be a private working document but can also circulate publicly.

The authors of CoMMA report 1.3 million manuscripts extant from the Latin West. For papyrus fragments, P. van Minnen estimated that between 1,000,000 and 1,500,000 are held in collections worldwide, fewer than 10% of which have been edited (van Minnen 2009: 644-645).

We believe that HTR might become an important research tool, particularly for unpublished texts, but also for published ones. It will complement other tools and technologies that have already been successfully integrated in papyrologists’ everyday work.

Examples of how AI-transcribed corpora can be used in (digital) humanities research are discussed in CoMMA. These include the computational analysis of the evolution of layouts, scribal practices, and palaeography, as well as the use of such corpora as a basis for developing further models and software (Clérice et al. 2026: §5). The same applications are also largely relevant to papyri. In this article, however, we focus on searching in an AI-transcribed corpus of unpublished papyri.

In September 2026, we retrieved digital images of unpublished papyri from collections in Vienna, Yale, Hamburg, and Bonn that are available online under open licenses
CC0 (Vienna, Yale, Bonn) and PDM 1.0 (Hamburg). and processed them using Anagnostes. The system had not been trained on any of these papyri and had never ‘seen’ them before this test. Processing each batch of 1,000 texts took approximately 50–60 minutes. The output was a corpus of line-by-line automated transcriptions of 9,370 papyri in the PAGE XML format.

Although we aimed to process only unpublished Greek texts, we did not manually verify or control the selection. Consequently, some papyri turned out to have already been published, despite the absence of this information in their metadata, while others contained texts in Coptic or Arabic. Nevertheless, this AI-transcribed corpus can already be searched using various methods, several of which we describe below alongside the findings they yielded. For each potential discovery, we also consulted the collection’s online catalogue and contacted the person responsible for the collection to ensure that the fragment is not already being edited. Since several interesting finds turned out to be already under study by other colleagues, we do not discuss them here.

Finally, although we tested all four search methods described below on the entire corpus of 9,370 papyri, we do not present all the results systematically. Instead, we discuss selected finds that illustrate how papyrus fragments within a single collection can be prioritised for publication. We do not compare results obtained across different collections. These searches should therefore be understood as case studies.

div.head: 4.1 Free-text keyword search: Four meaningful finds
div.p: We begin with the most straightforward and least sophisticated search method: searching the corpus for a word or combination of words of interest to the researcher, such as personal names, toponyms, special terms, and words indicative of a particular genre or content. We developed the search interface as part of our Papybench platform. It is not currently available online. In principle, the interface works in much the same way as papyri.info or any other full-text database search. One key difference is that it displays a snippet of the papyrus image showing the line in which the search term was found. This allows papyrologists to check immediately whether the automated transcription is correct.
[Fig. 1 Keyword search results interface showing image snippets from P.Vindob. Inv. G. 16003.]

To look for (the genre of) letters mentioned in papyri, we searched for the term ‘επιστολη’. The interface returned 29 results, 23 of which indeed contained this exact word. One of these, P.Vindob. Inv. G 16003, a fragment of a letter dating to the sixth/seventh c., will be published by E. Chepel in a forthcoming volume of ZPE.
[Fig. 2. Keyword search results interface showing image snippets from P.Vindob. Inv. G. 31642.]

We also searched for a combination of two words ‘χαιρειν’ and ‘μητρι᾽, to identify private letters addressed to a mother. This search returned 30 results, only one of which was actually a letter addressed to a mother, P.Vindob. Inv. G 31642. The description of this papyrus, prepared as part of the Mellon digitisation project in 2022, identifies it only as a letter. The word μητρί in the first line is obscured by a horizontal crack running in the middle of this line. It may have been overlooked by the scholar who prepared the catalogue description or simply not considered significant enough to be included among the keywords assigned to the fragment. In either case, the transcription produced by Anagnostes enabled us to identify this papyrus through a search targeting a specific genre and content – something that would not have been possible using the online catalogue of the Viennese collection alone.

To test a search for a rare term, we searched for the stem ‘καλαφατ’, hoping to find an unpublished text mentioning caulkers, workers who pitched the surface of boats and ships in Late antiquity. The search returned only one hit, which proved to be correct: a papyrus from the Yale collection, P.CtYBR inv.1749. This document is an account that can be dated to the fifth/sixth c. that lists payments to various workers, including caulkers, as well as other expenses, related to shipbuilding and repair. The online catalogue of the Yale papyrus collection identifies the document as an account and dates it to the sixth/seventh c., but provides no further information about its specific contents.

Finally, we tried a fuzzy search for ‘χειρογραφον’, which returned forty-three matches. By comparison, an exact-match search for this word returned only one papyrus. Fuzzy search broadens the search results by including texts in which the search word has been transcribed with errors. In this way, it helps mitigate transcription noise and address the problem of variant orthography in the original documents. The results of our search included the following variants in the automated transcriptions: χερογραφον, χειρογραφ, υπογραφον, ιδιογραφον, αντιγραφον, αγραφον, χειρογρ, χιρογραφον, χαιρογραφον, and others. The last of these, χαιρογραφον, results from a transcription error: Anagnostes mistook an epsilon in the papyrus for an alpha. This is a common error to which human readers are also prone. Nevertheless, this error in the automated transcription did not prevent us from finding documents that in fact contain the word χειρόγραφον. In one such document, P.CtYBR inv. 260, the word χειρόγραφον is damaged by a tear that affects three letters in the middle of the word: epsilon, iota, and rho. The catalogue of the Yale papyrus collection describes the document as a contract for the sale of land, but does not mention its private nature or the term cheirographon.

div.head: 4.2 Classification between documentary and literary texts: One significant find
div.p: For this type of search, we trained an additional model of the type TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency) on the corpus of documentary and literary texts available on papyri.info to determine whether a fragment comes from a documentary or literary text based on the vocabulary it contains (Repushko and Chepel, forthcoming: § 8.3). We then applied this model to our corpus of automated transcriptions. Of the approximately 300 unpublished papyri in the Bonn collection, we used the automatic transcriptions of 138 texts for this search, as we were able to retrieve only 138 images from the publicly available database.

The model classified two of these texts as literary. One of them, P.Bonn. Inv. 148, after it was manually compared with the corpus of Greek literary authors in the TLG, was identified as a biblical text: Psalm 34, verses 6-10. Using traditional papyrological methods, we further established that this papyrus belongs to the same roll as P.Lips. Inv. 39+P.Bonn. Inv. 147, which contains psalms 30-55 and was written on the verso of an account dated to 338 CE.

The Leipzig part was edited in Heinrici 1903 and re-edited in Emmenegger 2007; the small Bonn fragment was identified and published in Colomo and Scholl 2005. An edition of the newly identified Bonn fragment is being prepared by E. Chepel, Fritz Mitthof, and Amphilochios Papathomas.

In the catalogue of the Bonn collection, P. 148 is described as a documentary fragment of indeterminate content. At first glance, it does not look literary at all, and, without a hint, a papyrologist would be unlikely to compare this text with the TLG corpus. Rather, it looks more like a fragment of a private letter: it is written across the fibres on the verso of another document, in a cursive, somewhat untidy hand, and displays none of the features one might expect in a biblical text, such as nomina sacra. The vocabulary, too, does not initially suggest literary or biblical content. The only word that stands out and might be indicative is ψυχή, but this word also occurs in petitions and private letters.

This discovery demonstrates the genuine contribution that HTR can make to papyrology, as well as to biblical and early Chrisitan studies. It accelerates the identification of literary fragments that might otherwise remain unrecognised until a papyrologist undertakes a closer study and prepares an edition. However, a papyrus is much less likely to be selected for such study, if its significance has not yet been established.

div.head: 4.3 Text matching of automatic transcriptions against the corpus of Greek literature
div.p: In addition to applying a classification model to the corpus of first-hand transcriptions, it is possible to search all the automatic transcriptions against an existing, digitised, open-access corpus of texts of ancient Greek authors to identify textual matches. We applied this method to the unpublished papyri in Hamburg collection. The search identified a match between P.Hamb.Graec. Inv. 365 and Xen. Mem. 4.3. However, a manual check in Trismegistos revealed that this fragment had already been published in Chronopoulou 2024. The publication information, however, is missing from the corresponding record in the Hamburg database. Nevertheless, this result demonstrates that text matching can work successfully using transcriptions produced by Anagnostes.

div.head: 4.4 Searching with an LLM
div.p: An AI assistant based on a large language model (LLM), such as Claude Opus 5.5 or another model, can be asked to search an AI-transcribed corpus of unpublished papyri, with a prompt given in natural language. Breen used this approach to discover evidence of dodo hunting in the archive of the Dutch East India Company, as discussed above. He started with defining a specific research question, ran the transcribed handwritten sources through a semantic search to identify candidate passages that might help answer the research question; then asked a LLM to ‘read’ these passages, assess them from a historical perspective, and produce a ranked list of the best matches.

For our experiment search, we gave Claude Opus 5.5 a corpus of 326 papyri from the Hamburg collection, which had been automatically classified as unpublished on the basis of the metadata available online. We did not define a specific research question, as we wanted to test how the LLM would deal with the general task to find candidate fragments which can be prioritised for publication. In our prompt, we asked Claude to identify, using fuzzy search, the fragments in our corpus that seemed most interesting for publication and most promising from a papyrological perspective.
The criteria of what is interesting and promising where to be defined by Claude itself. When asked afterwards for a definition, it produced a reply which in our opinion would satisfy a papyrologist.

The two highest-ranked results, which the LLM deemed worthy of closer examination, were P.Hamb. Graec. Inv. 393 and P.Hamb. Graec. Inv. 153. The former was identified by the AI assistant as an unpublished complaint concerning forgery, addressed to the prefect of Egypt.
It turned out to be recently published in Pylon (Avdoulou and Sourlas 2026). We thank Thomas Ford for referring us to the publication. When asked to explain this attribution, the assistant cited the following phrases from the automatic transcription: “ψευδογραφ — false writing, forgery”; “ὑποθέσεων ἡγεμον” — “… of cases, the prefect”; and “ἀδικεῖν καὶ ἡμῖν ἐπηρεάζειν” — “… to wrong us and to harass us.”

Although the AI assistant correctly recognised the key terms, it silently changed the transcription produced by Anagnostes. In the last phrase, Anagnostes had correctly read an omicron at the beginning of line 17 of the papyrus (Fig. 3). The AI assistant, however, apparently deemed this reading erroneous and corrected the letter to an alpha, presumably on the basis of the more common verb ἀδικεῖν. It also normalised the spelling ἡμεῖν in the papyrus to ἡμῖν.

[Fig. 3. Anagnostes’ transcription of the line from P.Hamb. Graec. Inv. 393. Letters highlighted in red indicate a high level of uncertainty, while those highlighted in yellow indicate a medium to low level of uncertainty. Cf. the edition: [νται -ca.?- φυ]γ̣οδικεῖν καὶ ἡμεῖν ἐπηρεάζειν οὐκ οὖσιν.]

This papyrus was ranked by the AI assistant as the second most promising and interesting fragment for publication. This assessment is consistent with human expert judgement. When E. Chepel examined the Hamburg collection in 2023, she identified P.Hamb. Graec. Inv. 393 as a Roman petition that should be prioritised for publication. Thomas Ford, who has looked through the collection in search of pieces suitable to assign to students of papyrology school in Münster, also is of the opinion that this papyrus used to be “one of the more promising unedited pieces in the collection: fairly readable and fairly big” (per email).

The LLM’s top choice for publication among the unpublished papyri in the Hamburg collection was P.Hamb. Graec. Inv. 153. The AI assistant identified it as a Christian literary text, more specifically, a homily on a Gospel parable, possibly the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant (Matthew 18:23-35) or the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), since both passages mention debt and bankers, which are also referred to in the Hamburg fragment. The LLM correctly identified the hand as literary and recognised the presence of nomina sacra.

As in the previous case, its selection of this papyrus as a promising candidate for publication coincided with the judgement of a human expert: E. Chepel had also ranked it highly among the potentially interesting finds in the Hamburg collection, although she had identified it as a Christian letter rather than a literary text. P.Hamb. Graec. Inv. 153 has an address line on the verso which confirms that this papyrus is a letter. The surface in that place is too faded and abraded, and Anagnostes could not transcribe the text of the address. As a result, it was not present in the text corpus, and the LLM overlooked it and could not identify the genre correctly.

These two cases illustrate the limitations of using an LLM to identify interesting texts for further study. It is clear that human review of the candidates suggested by an LLM is always necessary. In future publications, we will test this search method using a more narrowly defined search request.

div.head: 5 Conclusions
div.p: The four types of search discussed here are just a few examples of the numerous research possibilities offered by AI-transcribed corpus of unpublished papyri. One method that we have not discussed here, but explored in our article for IJDAR, is the identification of document genres, for which either the HGV tags or the classification developed by Grammateus can be used.

Our aim in this article was not to provide an exhaustive list of the new methods and tools made possible by HTR technology. Nor did we compare the four search methods in detail, as this would require a thorough statistical analysis. Such an analysis is difficult to conduct given the limitations of the online images of unpublished papyri, which are not always readily accessible and often lack crucial metadata, such as publication status and assignment information. Future research would benefit from a case study involving a group of unpublished papyri and several papyrologists. Such a study could present its findings both quantitatively and qualitatively, highlight the most interesting AI-assisted discoveries, and systematically compare the results obtained by human experts working alone, machines working alone, and human experts assisted by machines.

In the present study, we have demonstrated that a tool such as Anagnostes can already in its current form contribute to the study of Greek papyri. Further improvements in HTR accuracy will lead to better search results. The design of searches, however, is neither predetermined by technology nor should it be. Rather, asking machines the right questions is a crucial part of the research process, and scholars should be free to formulate these questions according to their research interests, projects, and tasks. We hope that AI-driven HTR systems, with Anagnostes as a pioneering tool of its kind, will, when used critically and scientifically, lead to many exciting discoveries and breakthroughs in papyrology.
